en: Climbed the ridge and looked.
Hoping the boy was safe,
He raised the hare-foot spyglass in his hand;
Their elder, old Bakai,
Opening and closing one eye,
Looked for Semetey.
He saw him driving the herd with a roar,
Having raided it entire and whole.
Across Kaspang’s Kara-Talaa,
Countless black shapes like ants
Spread glittering over the plain.
The accursed one had taken many animals,
Not merely a few, but an abundance.
Their hoofbeats made the heavens resound;
He had taken an endless mass of stock.
He had begun his fury fiercely,
And slaughtered all the feeble ones,
Leaving them along the road.
Swaying and streaming onward,
The barren mares led the herd;
He had sent the foals shivering
And killed them in the water.
The whinnying brood mares
He drove along with heavy steps.
At Echoing Zhar-Kyya,
They began to file out one by one;
They streamed over the great ridge.
When they came into that procession,
Not one horse remained outside the file.
Their elder Bakai examined
The horses Semetey had brought.
He flared up in anger,
And in his old age mighty Bakai
Found grief waiting before him.
His wail split the stones,
His cry split heads,
And he halted at Kapka-Tash.
His heart smoked fiercely with grief,
And he mourned the days gone by.
As though held fast in place,
Semetey, behind the herd,
Stopped before Khan Bakai.
Poor Bakai wept long:
“My gray-maned Manas, companion of my youth,
If only you had not died!” he wept.
“Manas, my companion, sharer of my soul,
Parted from you, my soul’s companion,
You are nowhere among the living,
Yet nowhere in the grave if called dead.
With a wail that splits stone,
Your Bakai wanders distraught.
When that Manas was alive,
Why did I not then behold
The ground below, like Judgment Day?
When my lion, my gray-maned wolf, was alive,
Why did I not die then?
O beard of one who felled the foe,
Parted from my tiger,
Is this your time to lie upon the ridge?!
When my black-steel Zulfiqar
Hung smoking at my side,
When I drove back
All who attacked,
When I kept my sharp, lamb-ribbed spear
Bound ready at my side;
When I drove back many peoples,
To say nothing of the Chinese;
When my world was wide, not narrowed,
In the time of fortunate Manas—
Why did I not die then?
When, if bored, we hunted deer,
And if not, in Talas
We passed our days in freedom;
When I wore my paired sable cap
And set it jauntily,
Lamenting and singing with the hero,
With my dear lion Manas,
When I lived in joy—
Why did I not die here then?
My long-suffering Manas, if only you had not died,
My sheep sharing one fold,
My food sharing one circle of companions.
My valiant Manas, if only you had not died,
So Bakai need not whiten a beard like a swan,
Nor redden eyes like a raven’s,
Nor live to see this torment.
Who did not cock the sable cap upon his head
And wear it with a flourish?
When strength remained in his arm,
Who did not walk the earth roaring?
Before that noble soul’s venom,
Did the Kakan’s people not tremble?
Even distant Beijing, beyond a stallion’s reach,
We fought until we made it submit;
It was an army that trampled
The swaggering Kalcha.
We scattered the army he had gathered,
And when we cast Beijing into turmoil,
We took the daughters of Beijing’s lords
And carried them away as prizes.
Why did I not die then?
Great Beijing, that city with its court—
We broke Beijing and took its realm,
Loaded gold pieces upon camels,
And took a thousand dark-eyed maidens.
My name, Bakai, split the stones;
When I was mighty and strong,
Why did I not die then?
When the pitch-black city’s ruler
I held surrounded,
When I beat the black Chinese and many Manchus,
Roasting their people like wheat,
And scourged them;
When, in this accursed false world,
My wing, Manas, was still beside me,
Why did I not perish then?
Ah, my son Semetey,
May you be ruined if you call this taking horses!
Among the swarming Chinese,
One who slaughtered the people and took their herds—
Could he have an heir like you?
Can anyone prosper who calls you a living man?
My son, had you never been born, sink into darkness;
Rather than live, go and die!
Drink stones instead of liquor;
And if that is too little, my foal,
Mix in your elder Bakai’s blood and drink!
You boast without cause,
Saying you went to make war
Upon the innumerable Chinese,
Saying you raided the horses
Of a Kalda who lived out on the frontier.
There is no stallion and no riding horse,
Not one fit to mount in battle.
Be swept away together with your herd!
The devils you have driven here
Belong to a half-lunged Kalda;
Deceived in a wretched place,
Could a champion be like you?
Has anyone who calls you a hero
Ever prospered since ancient times?
You have driven here
The lice swarming at his collar;
They are all unbroken colts and fillies—
You have driven here his dogs.
From the sleeping Kalmak
You have driven here his cows;
From the Kalda lying in a hollow,
You have driven here his sheep.
Among the horses you brought,
There is no mount fit for a firefight,
Not one fit to ride on campaign!
Rather than raid horses of this sort,
Could you not have returned empty-handed,
Saying, “Fighting the black Kalmak,
My strength failed me,”
And come back ruined?
You rejoice, it seems,
Saying you have taken many horses—
Yet my noble lion Manas, companion of my youth,
Could have urinated upon stones at your age!
If only Manas had died before he was born!
My noble son, look upon
These horses you have driven here!
Does a hero not die of shame?
When fate casts it upon his head,
Does a doomed young man not see it?
Among all these horses,
There is not one fine beast
To ride with graceful bearing
At a memorial feast or celebration;
There is not one fit to gird on the Zhozhura sword
And circle the face of the earth,
Not one beast fit to ride into conflict.
Though you pull the saddle girth tight,
There is not one fit to ride into battle!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
Muradyl had raided away their horses,
And when we drove them on foot, they would not walk;
If we mounted them behind us, there was no room,
So the two were left on foot in the steppe.
They thought their elder would raid horses,
And drive them back toward us;
They hoped he would take
At least one thoroughbred racing horse, unless he were a dog.
The hopes of those two
Were dashed against stone on the steppe.
Semetey, in whom I placed my hope—
My son, despairing of you,
Bakai’s mouth has fallen closed.
He was your equal, your companion in age;
Parted from the companion of his own age,
This Bakai standing here—
What a variety I said!
The mare took the net,
You've had enough
Take a slave with a slave,
Will you be the one chasing revenge?! –
Saying, the old man Bakay,
Sad tune,
Speaking to Semetei,
Pulling out his beard and throwing it away
Twisting his mustache and throwing
Golden cheeks,
Leaning on an empty stomach,
Dear Manas, don't die.
His white beard is thinning,
Tears flowing down two faces,
Uncle Bakay Kargan,
Poured down slowly,
Sweet soul says to die
It is hard to come in.
Your grandfather, Kargan Bakay,
Sad horse
Kutpa drove the side.
Semetey fell under it,
He is brave, he has no sense,
Know the tenderness from this,
What is a man out of the blue?
Father Manas is from Kojjal,
What is the relative of the rear?
To the place of rebellion,
A sycamore is planted like a yard,
I am descended from Ukuman
He supported from the beginning.
Dear Taibuurul,
Take the hangover,
Are you in the news?
Akkelte summer is like this,
Every side of Anjiyan,
As for Amangen,
The domain of Kokon Khan,
From Idai Sary-Talaa,
Sixty Russian land surveyors,
When the special comes out,
The air of Kiran Bakay,
The day before the ambassador came down,
When the Russian does not give,
All in a row,
Wearing yellow
All in a row,
who owns his slaves,
Riding a wild mare,
Eighty sunny days,
A beautiful old man,
Akkelte received from Kerish
Ochogor when playing
Actually Koychakir,
Surplus iron Almabash,
Indestructible in sixty days.
You are four months pregnant,
Estimated location,
If a shot comes out of his mouth
If not alive.
Father Manas is from noble-hearted.
Akkelte, the depositor,
